title: God's goodness, justice, and knowledge of all things
english: For if, he says, love for humanity is not seen in all things, but many painful and destructive things accompany what is pleasant and saving—such as failure of crops, the birth of deadly beasts, and the onsets of diseases—yet none of these is outside righteousness, which is beautifully interwoven with goodness so that zeal for what is good is not corrupted by the unrebuked cheerfulness of those who break the law (Ps 144:21).

Again he stretches his praises to a great length and does not stop at one person or his own person, but he will do the same for all people [...] into the endless age, if he too will one day see with those who run, showing that they share in the company of the righteous who have become a beginning for God, according to the apostle (Ps 145:1-2).

He seems to teach that this is the work of life, this is the benefit of existing—if we are joined to true life and to the one who truly is (Ps 145:5). For this is a provision both for true life and for existing eternally, since we carry with us from this present life a provision for the life to come.

So hope in humans is wretched, but hope in God is blessed. For he is a true helper, eternal and holding power over all things (Ps 146:4). In him is the authority, as from ungrudging wealth and boundless resources, to do great good easily.

He is so great and so vast that not even the countless stars are outside his knowledge, but having been ordered by him, they are known to him precisely, since he distinguishes the nature and power of each one as by names that mark them off (Ps 146:5).

title: God's power and wisdom as begotten, not accidental
english: Strength then and understanding—even if we hear these in human terms, let us not think humanly about what kind of strength it is by which a strong man acts, and what kind of understanding it is by which a wise man deliberates, since he has power and wisdom that come and go. For as God he is not powerful and wise in that way, since he does not even have anything better or lesser in himself—such as power and what is filled with power, wisdom and what is full of wisdom—but he is entirely the most perfect, and for this reason he does not have power and wisdom that fill him, but full, proceeding from himself. Just as Solomon calls wisdom an offspring and presents wisdom-itself as having come from God, and by saying that the works of creation were made by wisdom he teaches that the begetter of wisdom is something greater than the direct work of creation. To him belongs the great superiority that has risen above any connection with created things by its presence to the one who creates, since it is impossible to conceive of anything greater than the greatest. So what is conceived as greatest, by having surpassed every relation to created things, is what belongs to the Father of wisdom and power. And so great is his strength and his understanding, as being from him and with him an offspring and fruit and son, not as an accident in him—concerning which it is said, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Then, since this power is also wisdom, having the same name as the understanding in which he made the heaven, according to what was said, “To him who made the heaven in understanding” (Psalm 135:5 (136:5)), his strength and understanding are great beyond number, and the understanding of God is untraceable. Hence it is written, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and ... [text breaks off]” (Romans 11:33).

title: God's knowledge beyond number and the praise of angels, lights, and saints
english: of the knowledge of God. For since his understanding is deepest, because of its incomprehensibility it has no number. And if it is also said to have no number because of the surpassing multitude of the contemplations in it, you yourself will also understand.

The angels would be those in the heavens, and the powers are above even these, belonging to the highest places, being above the task of bringing messages to human beings, and having their blessedness in perpetual steadfastness with God alone (Ps 148:2). Such also are the thrones, which the apostle calls, the name indicating that God is seated upon them, and that they are subject to the divine majesty that is above creation, standing always in this and having their fixed and stable state in the reception of the divine glory.

The lights that shine in the heaven by day and by night, illuminating the heaven itself, the highest one—that is, the firmament according to Moses—and also the water above this, are commanded to praise God. It is clear that all these things are a hymn of God, displaying in their own beauty and power and activity the all-hymned nature of their Maker.

And by saying “holy ones” he indicates those from every nation (Ps 148:14). Then, bringing in Israel by prophecy because it had drawn near from the beginning, he shows that its following comes after the nations.

The word necessarily prophesied for those who have fallen asleep the rest after death and the exultation in it, according to the verse, “In peace I will lie down and sleep” (Psalm 4:9 (4:8)) (Ps 149:5).
